items.title: Europe joins global stock market rally as AI trade rebounds - as it happened
items.summary:
Rolling coverage of the latest economic and financial news

It looks like it will be a strong open later in the US market – futures for the tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 are up 2.7% as optimism around the AI trade returns.

Shares in the memory company SanDisk are up 11% in pre-market trading. Nvidia is up 4%, while Micron and Marvell Technology are both up by about 7% in pre-market.

Following this revision, the annual growth carry-over for 2026 stands at only 0.1%. It is very difficult to see domestic demand rebounding strongly enough in the fourth quarter to improve this result.

Business and consumer confidence both deteriorated in October and November. A weakening labour market and growing fears of unemployment will keep households cautious. At the same time, weak demand and a lack of visibility will continue to weigh on business investment.

This would leave average GDP growth at just 0.1% in 2026, well below the 1.0% we expect for the eurozone.

The outlook for 2027 remains very gloomy. Salaried employment fell by 94,400 jobs over the past year, a decline of 0.3%. The situation is even worse in the private sector, where 109,000 jobs were lost over the same period, a fall of 0.5%.

Hannah Webster, senior economist at the think tank New Economics Foundation, also called for other measures.

The price cap increase will be difficult news for households to bear, especially during the winter when our energy needs and bills are higher. The government’s current support measures don’t match the reality of rising costs and squeezed household finances.

The £100 payment announced at the budget won’t cover the increase that’s coming, nor is it available to every household. According to NEF analysis, one million low-income households will miss out.

Today’s price cap rise shows how exposed households remain to imported energy - the answer is to generate more at home.

Biomethane, made from farms and food waste, is already flowing through our grid - enough to heat around a million homes - but NESO [National Energy System Operator] has just cut its outlook for biomethane because of policy uncertainty.

items.title: Compass’s logic for US listing is flimsy but UK ministers need to wake up to Footsie flight risk | Nils Pratley
items.summary:
The contract caterer switching to New York is a big hit to the London Stock Exchange but what is being done to discourage others from delisting?

That’s gratitude, eh? Compass Group built its business, in part, on contracts to serve dinners in British schools and run catering operations in NHS hospitals. Now it plans to switch its primary stock market listing to New York in 2028.

Compass is a bad one for the London market to lose. First, it is the 18th largest company in the FTSE 100 index and one of the few that is the biggest in the world in its market (contract catering, not just for the public sector but for thousands of corporate clients). Second, its reasons for joining the stateside listing rush feel flimsy – but also dangerous.

Zohran Mamdani, New York City’s mayor, on Monday weighed in on the corporate turbulence surrounding Nvidia and the chipmaker’s chief executive officer, Jensen Huang, saying he does not think working Americans “signed up for their pensions being tied to the question of … Huang’s fidelity to his marriage”.

The mayor said Huang “had a massive impact”, with Nvidia’s share price dropping dramatically when Huang stepped down as the company’s CEO on 12 November after a reported extramarital relationship with a suspected Chinese spy.

Shares in UK housebuilder Crest Nicholson have slumped by a quarter, to a record low, after the company issued a profits warning this morning.

Full year completions were 1,353, at the bottom end of the Group’s previous guidance range of 1,350 to 1,400 completions.

The warning has hammered Crest Nicholson shares, which have lost more than a quarter of their value this morning, currently trading down over 30%. The brutal sell-off is also weighing on the wider sector, dragging peers like Barratt Redrow, Persimmon, Vistry and Bellway into the red.

Today’s update suggests that weakness in the housing market is no longer confined to first-time buyers. Crest Nicholson is predominantly exposed to the mid-premium family housing market, and the sharp deterioration in sales rates indicates that more affluent upsizers are also becoming increasingly cautious amid macroeconomic and geopolitical uncertainty.

items.title: Anthropic’s IPO was great for the tech elite – and not so great for the rest of us | Steven Greenhouse
items.summary:
The company’s co-founders are now wildly rich, while countless Americans face AI-driven threats to their jobs and fears of a stock bubble

The sultans of Silicon Valley and the wizards of Wall Street rejoiced this week when Anthropic raised an eye-popping $81bn in the largest initial public offering in history. They saw the AI company’s IPO as a gung-ho affirmation of Silicon Valley’s and Wall Street’s marriage of technology and capitalism.

For many employees at the company that developed Claude, the public offering must have been a thing of dreams. With the IPO valuing Anthropic at $1.5tn, the company’s seven co-founders each came away with stakes worth about $20bn, while, by one estimate, 600 of Anthropic’s more than 5,000 employees will have holdings topping $100m and 2,800 others will have shares worth more than $10m.
